claim: Human speech comprehension involves incrementally integrating consecutive words into a structured and coherent interpretation, aligning with the speaker's intended meaning.
source: A core aspect of human speech comprehension is the ability to incrementally integrate consecutive words into a structured and coherent interpretation, aligning with the speaker's intended meaning.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about speech comprehension supported by established scientific consensus in psycholinguistics and cognitive science.

claim: Speech comprehension is subject to multidimensional probabilistic constraints, including both linguistic knowledge and non-linguistic information within specific contexts.
source: This rapid process is subject to multidimensional probabilistic constraints, including both linguistic knowledge and non-linguistic information within specific contexts, and it is their interpretative coherence that drives successful comprehension.
evidence: This claim is supported by the constraint-based approach to sentence processing discussed in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: BERT, a deep language model, effectively approximates the coherent outcomes of the dynamic interplay among various types of constraints in speech comprehension.
source: To study the neural substrates of this process, we extract word-by-word measures of sentential structure from BERT, a deep language model, which effectively approximates the coherent outcomes of the dynamic interplay among various types of constraints.
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation analyses presented in the manuscript showing correlations between BERT measures and human behavioral data.

claim: The incremental construction of structured interpretations engages bilateral brain regions extending beyond the classical fronto-temporal language system.
source: These findings show when and where coherent interpretations emerge through the evaluation and integration of multifaceted constraints in the brain, which engages bilateral brain regions extending beyond the classical fronto-temporal language system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results showing activations in multiple brain regions including the default mode network and multiple-demand network.

claim: Individual words are combined according to non-linear and often discontinuous structure embedded in an utterance as it is delivered over time.
source: Crucially, rather than simple linear concatenation, individual words are combined according to the non-linear and often discontinuous structure embedded in an utterance as it is delivered over time (Everaert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Everaert et al., 2015 and illustrated by the example sentence provided.

claim: In the sentence 'The boy who chased the cat was …', it is the structurally close word 'boy', rather than the linearly close word 'cat', that is combined with 'was'.
source: For example, in the sentence "The boy who chased the cat was …", it is the structurally close word 'boy', rather than the linearly close word 'cat', that is combined with 'was'.
evidence: This is a linguistic example demonstrating structural dependency that is established knowledge in syntax.

claim: Finding the structure in an unfolding sentence depends on constraints jointly placed by linguistic properties and non-linguistic information such as broad world knowledge.
source: Nevertheless, finding the structure in an unfolding sentence also depends on the constraints jointly placed by other linguistic properties and non-linguistic information such as the broad world knowledge (Bever, 1970; Tyler and Marslen-Wilson, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bever, 1970 and Tyler and Marslen-Wilson, 1977.

claim: The constraint-based approach to sentence processing proposes that speech comprehension is concurrently governed by multiple types of probabilistic constraints generated by individual words as they are sequentially heard.
source: Unlike the two-stage model (Frazier, 1987; Frazier and Rayner, 1982) which posits an initial parsing stage relying solely on syntax, the constraint-based approach to sentence processing (MacDonald et al., 1994; Trueswell and Tanenhaus, 1994) proposes that speech comprehension is concurrently governed by multiple types of probabilistic constraints (e.g. syntax, semantics, world knowledge), generated by individual words as they are sequentially heard.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MacDonald et al., 1994 and Trueswell and Tanenhaus, 1994.

claim: There is no delay in the utilization of multifaceted constraints once they become available in speech comprehension.
source: There is no delay in the utilization of these multifaceted constraints once they become available, neither is a fixed priority assigned to one type of constraint over another; rather, it is the interpretative coherence of all available constraints that forms the basis for successful language comprehension (Altmann, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Altmann, 1998 and represents a key tenet of the constraint-based approach.

claim: Contemporary deep language models have made great strides in natural language processing tasks including text generation, parsing, and translation.
source: Contemporary deep language models (DLMs) have made great strides in a wide array of natural language processing tasks, including text generation, parsing, and translation (Vaswani, 2017; Devlin et al., 2019; Brown, 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple papers on deep language models.

claim: Current deep language models are imperfect in terms of human-level language understanding related to reasoning and complex physical or social situations.
source: While current DLMs are still imperfect in terms of human-level language understanding related to reasoning and complex physical or social situations (Bisk et al., 2020), they are arguably valuable models of general linguistic capacities due to their ability to identify and leverage relevant statistical regularities of linguistic and non-linguistic world knowledge present in massive training data (Linzen and Baroni, 2021; Pavlick, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bisk et al., 2020, Linzen and Baroni, 2021, and Pavlick, 2022.

claim: Deep language models excel in flexible combination of different types of features embedded in their rich internal representations.
source: In this regard, DLMs excel in flexible combination of different types of features (e.g. syntactic structure and semantic meaning) embedded in their rich internal representations (Linzen and Baroni, 2021; Pavlick, 2022; Bengio et al., 2021; Manning et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Linzen and Baroni, 2021; Pavlick, 2022; Bengio et al., 2021; and Manning et al., 2020.

claim: Recent studies have revealed an overall congruence between language representations in deep language models and those observed in the human brain while processing the same spoken or written input.
source: Recent studies have revealed an overall congruence between language representations in DLMs and those observed in the human brain while processing the same spoken or written input (Schrimpf et al., 2021; Goldstein et al., 2022; Heilbron et al., 2022; Toneva et al., 2022; Caucheteux et al., 2022; Caucheteux and King, 2022; Caucheteux et al., 2023), suggesting the potential value of DLMs as a computational tool to investigate the neural basis of language comprehension.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple recent studies on brain-model alignment.

claim: Sixty sets of sentences with varying sentential structures were constructed for the study.
source: We constructed 60 sets of sentences with varying sentential structures (see 'Materials and methods') and presented them to human listeners.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental stimuli.

claim: In each stimulus set, there are two target sentences differing only in the transitivity of the first verb (Verb1) encountered.
source: In each stimulus set, there are two target sentences differing only in the transitivity of the first verb (Verb1) encountered, that is, how likely it is that Verb1 takes a direct object
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental design.

claim: The structural interpretation of sentences is ambiguous at the point Verb1 is encountered.
source: Critically, the structural interpretation of these sentences is ambiguous at the point Verb1 is encountered, and the preferred human resolution of this ambiguity depends on the real-time integration of linguistic and non-linguistic constraints as more of the sentence is heard.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and the behavioral data from continuation pre-tests.

claim: The sequence 'The dog found …' could initially have either an active interpretation or a passive interpretation.
source: In the example above, the sequence "The dog found …" could initially have either an active interpretation – where the dog has found something – or a passive interpretation – where the dog is found by someone (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is illustrated by the example and Figure 1.

claim: Because 'find' is primarily a transitive verb, the human listener is likely to be biased towards an initial active interpretation.
source: Because 'find' is primarily a transitive verb, the human listener is likely to be biased towards an initial active interpretation.
evidence: This claim is based on linguistic knowledge about verb transitivity and its effect on interpretation.

claim: The initial structural interpretation up to Verb1 depends on non-linguistic information about how likely the subject is to adopt the active (agent) role to perform the specified action.
source: This initial structural interpretation up to Verb1 does not, however, just depend on linguistic knowledge such as Verb1 transitivity. It also depends on non-linguistic information, that is, how likely the subject is (or is not) to adopt the active (agent) role to perform the specified action (Dowty, 1991; Marslenwilson et al., 1993), that is, 'thematic role' properties of the subject noun.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dowty, 1991 and Marslenwilson et al., 1993.

claim: The active interpretation should be more strongly favoured in 'The king found/walked …' given the higher agenthood of the 'king'.
source: So, regardless of Verb1 transitivity, the active interpretation should be more strongly favoured in "The king found/walked …" given the higher agenthood of the 'king' and thus the greater implausibility of a passive interpretation involving a 'king' relative to a 'dog'.
evidence: This is an inference based on world knowledge about thematic roles.

claim: The passive interpretation becomes more preferred in a HiTrans sentence as the prepositional phrase is processed, given the absence of an expected direct object.
source: Specifically, the passive interpretation will become more preferred in a HiTrans sentence, given the absence of an expected direct object for the highly transitive Verb1, so Verb1 tends to be interpreted as a passive verb [i.e. the head of a reduced relative clause in "The dog (that was) found in the park …"].
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and behavioral data.

claim: In a LoTrans sentence, the active interpretation of Verb1 is strengthened by the incoming prepositional phrase.
source: Conversely, in a LoTrans sentence, the active interpretation of Verb1 is strengthened by the incoming prepositional phrase, which is in accord with the verb's intransitive use and the event conjured up by the sequence of words heard so far (e.g. "The dog walked in the park …").
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and behavioral data.

claim: With the appearance of the actual main verb, the active interpretation of Verb1 as the main verb is completely rejected in both HiTrans and LoTrans sentences.
source: However, with the appearance of the actual main verb (e.g. 'was covered' in the example sentences), the active interpretation of Verb1 as the main verb will be completely rejected, which resolves the potential ambiguity and confirms the passive interpretation in both HiTrans and LoTrans sentences.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and the structure of the stimulus sentences.

claim: A direct object was more likely to be found in HiTrans sentences in the continuations after Verb1.
source: In the continuations after Verb1, a direct object was more likely to be found in HiTrans sentences, indicating a transitive use of Verb1, while an opposite pattern was found for a PP continuation, indicating an intransitive use of Verb1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the continuation pre-test shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The probability of a main verb in the continuations after the prepositional phrase was lower in LoTrans sentences.
source: As expected, the probability of a main verb (MV) in the continuations after the prepositional phrase was lower in LoTrans sentences (Figure 2C), suggesting that listeners preferred the active interpretation and tended to interpret Verb1 as the main verb by the end of the prepositional phrase in LoTrans sentences, and vice versa in HiTrans sentences.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the continuation pre-test shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Neither of the two pre-tests resulted in a complete separation between HiTrans and LoTrans sentences; instead, they were characterized by two different but overlapping probabilistic distributions.
source: Crucially, neither of the two pre-tests resulted in a complete separation between HiTrans and LoTrans sentences; instead, they were characterized by two different but overlapping probabilistic distributions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data from the continuation pre-tests.

claim: Human interpretative preference for the two types of sentences was significantly correlated with the lexical constraints placed by the subject noun and Verb1.
source: In accord with the constraint-based hypothesis, we found that human interpretative preference for the two types of sentences was significantly correlated with the lexical constraints placed by the subject noun and Verb1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BERT parse depth of words at the same position formed a distribution ranging around the corresponding context-free parse depths in either the passive or the active interpretation.
source: We found that, for each type of sentences, the BERT parse depth of words at the same position formed a distribution ranging around the corresponding context-free parse depths in either the passive or the active interpretation (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting a word-specific rather than position-specific structural representation.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of BERT parse depths shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Content words contributed significantly more than function words to the variances encoded in BERT parse depth vectors.
source: Our analysis revealed that content words contributed significantly more than function words (i.e. the determiners) (see Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the shuffling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: HiTrans sentences continuously moved towards the passive interpretation landmark after Verb1, with a significant change of distances detected at the main verb.
source: As shown by the trajectories of the median BERT parse depth of the two sentence types (see the lower panel of Figure 3D), in general, HiTrans sentences continuously moved towards the passive interpretation landmark after Verb1, with a significant change of distances detected at the main verb (see the orange bars in Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: LoTrans sentences started by approaching the active interpretation landmark but were reorientated to the passive counterpart with the appearance of the actual main verb.
source: LoTrans sentences started by approaching the active interpretation landmark but were reorientated to the passive counterpart with the appearance of the actual main verb, with significant changes of distances detected at both Verb1 and main verb (see the purple bars in Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: From the incoming prepositional phrase to the main verb, sentences that are closer to the passive landmark in the model space have higher Verb1 transitivity, a higher passive index but a lower active index.
source: Consistently, from the incoming prepositional phrase to the main verb, sentences that are closer to the passive landmark in the model space have higher Verb1 transitivity, a higher passive index but a lower active index, while sentences closer to the active interpretation landmark exhibited higher active index and lower passive index (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: At the beginning of the prepositional phrase, the change of distance towards either interpretation landmark between two consecutive words is correlated with lexical constraints.
source: Moreover, at the beginning of the prepositional phrase, the change of distance towards either interpretation landmark between two consecutive words is also correlated with these constraints (Figure 4C and D), suggesting an immediate update in the structural interpretation in combination with the accumulated constraints from the preceding subject noun and Verb1.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Both the incremental BERT parse depth vectors as a whole and the BERT parse depth of Verb1 are correlated with the constraints placed by the subject noun and Verb1.
source: Moreover, we found that both the incremental BERT parse depth vectors as a whole (which are captured by their principal components) and the BERT parse depth of Verb1 (which is the most indicative marker of the interpretation preferred) are correlated with the constraints placed by the subject noun and Verb1 (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: BERT structural interpretations were correlated with the main verb probability in the continuation pre-test which directly reflects human interpretation preference.
source: In addition, we found that BERT structural interpretations were also correlated with the main verb probability in the continuation pre-test which directly reflects human interpretation preference (black bars in Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 4.

claim: The incremental BERT parse depth vectors exhibited significant fits to brain activity consistently in all three epochs as the corresponding word was being heard.
source: We found that the incremental BERT parse depth vectors exhibited significant fits to brain activity consistently in all three epochs as the corresponding word was being heard at that time (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: In Verb1 epoch, effects in bilateral frontal and anterior-to-middle temporal regions started immediately from Verb1 onset and continued until the uniqueness point.
source: In Verb1 epoch, effects in bilateral frontal and anterior-to-middle temporal regions started immediately from Verb1 onset and continued until the uniqueness point – the point at which the word has been uniquely identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Effects of BERT parse depth vectors were found in the left fronto-temporal regions in the two later epochs, starting after the recognition of the preposition or the main verb separately.
source: As the sentence unfolded, effects of BERT parse depth vectors were found in the left fronto-temporal regions in the two later epochs, starting after the recognition of the preposition or the main verb separately.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Only the mismatch for active interpretation showed significant effects in Verb1 epoch.
source: Turning to the interpretative mismatch for the two possible interpretations, we only observed significant effects of the mismatch for active interpretation in Verb1 epoch (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The mismatch for passive interpretation fitted brain activity in the preposition and main verb epochs.
source: However, it was the mismatch for passive interpretation that fitted brain activity in the preposition and main verb epochs (Figure 6E and F, marginal significance in main verb epoch with cluster-wise p=0.06).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Listeners, in general, tended to have an initial preference for an active interpretation but might start favouring a passive interpretation when the prepositional phrase began to be heard.
source: These results suggest that listeners, in general, tended to have an initial preference for an active interpretation (even before the recognition of Verb1) but might start favouring a passive interpretation when the prepositional phrase began to be heard.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of neural effects for interpretative mismatch.

claim: This finding is consistent with the tendency to process the first noun encountered at the beginning of a sentence as the agent.
source: This finding is consistent with the tendency to process the first noun encountered at the beginning of a sentence as the agent (Bever, 1970; Jackendoff, 2002; Mahowald et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bever, 1970; Jackendoff, 2002; and Mahowald et al., 2023.

claim: Across the three epochs, the most sustained effects were observed in the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and the anterior temporal lobe (ATL).
source: Across the three epochs, the most sustained effects were observed in the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and the anterior temporal lobe (ATL).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6.

claim: With the identification of the actual main verb, effects of the eventually resolved structure also involved regions in the left prefrontal and inferior parietal regions which belong to the multiple-demand network.
source: Notably, with the identification of the actual main verb, effects of the eventually resolved structure also involved regions in the left prefrontal and inferior parietal regions (Figure 6C) which belong to the multiple-demand network (Duncan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6C and citation to Duncan, 2010.

claim: The involvement of the prefrontal regions could be indicative of the varying working memory demands for building the structure of the unfolding sentence.
source: The involvement of the prefrontal regions could be indicative of the varying working memory demands (e.g. the different number of open nodes in the sentence structures for active and passive interpretations before the actual main verb is recognized) for building the structure of the unfolding sentence (Nelson et al., 2017; Pallier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Nelson et al., 2017 and Pallier et al., 2011.

claim: Significant fits to brain activity for the change of Verb1 parse depth emerged in the left posterior temporal and inferior parietal regions upon the main verb uniqueness point.
source: We first tested the change of Verb1 parse depth in the main verb epoch. Significant fits to brain activity emerged in the left posterior temporal and inferior parietal regions upon the main verb uniqueness point, and then extended to more anterior temporal regions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: After the main verb offset, the declining effects of the Verb1 parse depth change in the left anterior temporal region seamlessly overlapped with the arising effects of the updated Verb1 parse depth.
source: After the main verb offset, the declining effects of the Verb1 parse depth change in the left anterior temporal region seamlessly overlapped with the arising effects of the updated Verb1 parse depth (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: The left hippocampus was activated for both measures of Verb1 parse depth after the actual main verb is recognized.
source: It is also worth noting that the left hippocampus was activated for both measures of Verb1 parse depth after the actual main verb is recognized, suggesting that the episodic memory of experienced events might contribute to the updating of structural interpretations (Bicknell et al., 2010; Altmann and Ekves, 2019; Metusalem et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results and citations to Bicknell et al., 2010; Altmann and Ekves, 2019; and Metusalem et al., 2012.

claim: Significant effects of agenthood were found in the preposition epoch.
source: We first tested the subject noun thematic role properties obtained from corpus data. Significant effects of agenthood and patienthood were found in the preposition epoch (Figure 8A) and in the main verb epoch (Figure 8B) separately.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Significant effects of patienthood were found in the main verb epoch.
source: Significant effects of agenthood and patienthood were found in the preposition epoch (Figure 8A) and in the main verb epoch (Figure 8B) separately.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Effects of the subject noun itself preceded those of incremental BERT parse depth vectors modelling the sentence fragments in the same epoch.
source: Notably, effects of the subject noun itself preceded those of incremental BERT parse depth vectors modelling the sentence fragments in the same epoch (compare Figure 8A with Figure 6B and Figure 8B with Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing the timing of effects in Figure 8A with Figure 6B and Figure 8B with Figure 6C.

claim: Subject noun thematic role might be evaluated before building the overall structural interpretation of the utterance delivered so far.
source: These findings indicate that subject noun thematic role might be evaluated before building the overall structural interpretation of the utterance delivered so far.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal ordering of neural effects.

claim: Effects of the non-directional measure of interpretative coherence appeared very soon after the main verb onset in both hemispheres and lasted till its offset.
source: Effects of this non-directional measure of interpretative coherence appeared very soon after the main verb onset in both hemispheres and lasted till its offset (Figure 8C), suggesting an immediate evaluation of the previously integrated constraints from the subject noun and Verb1 when a listener realized that the sentence had not finished yet.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The most sustained regions associated with the non-directional index, including the left ATL, angular gyrus (AG), and precuneus, are classical areas of the default mode network.
source: Intriguingly, the most sustained regions associated with this non-directional index, including the left ATL, angular gyrus (AG), and precuneus, are also the classical areas of the DMN. This finding is consistent with recent claims that the DMN integrates external input with internal prior knowledge to make sense of an input stimulus such as speech (Yeshurun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results and citation to Yeshurun et al., 2021.

claim: Precuneus and angular gyrus have been found to be involved in building thematic relationships and event structures.
source: In particular, precuneus and AG have been found to be involved in building thematic relationships and event structures (Baldassano et al., 2017; Humphreys et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baldassano et al., 2017 and Humphreys et al., 2021.

claim: Significant effects of the passive index were found in right anterior fronto-temporal regions following the declining effects of the non-directional index upon the recognition of the main verb.
source: Following the declining effects of the non-directional index upon the recognition of the main verb, we found significant effects of the passive index in right anterior fronto-temporal regions (Figure 8D), suggesting that the intended passive interpretation was eventually established in all sentences.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Previous studies have revealed that the relatively narrow sentence-specific information and the broad world knowledge are processed in the left and right hemispheres separately.
source: Previous studies have revealed that the relatively narrow sentence-specific information and the broad world knowledge are processed in the left and right hemispheres separately (Jung-Beeman, 2005; Metusalem et al., 2016; Troyer et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jung-Beeman, 2005; Metusalem et al., 2016; and Troyer et al., 2022.

claim: In the main verb epoch, effects of the BERT parse depth vector and those of the passive index in the left and right hemispheres arose almost at the same time as the main verb was recognized.
source: Relevant to this, in the main verb epoch, we found effects of the BERT parse depth vector and those of the passive index in the left and right hemispheres, respectively, arising almost at the same time as the main verb was recognized (compare Figure 6C and Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing the timing of effects in Figure 6C and Figure 8D.

claim: Granger causality analysis identified information flows from the right hemisphere components of the passive index to the left hemisphere components of BERT parse depth vector.
source: We found only GC connections from the components of passive index to those of BERT parse depth vector (Figure 8E). Specifically, we identified information flows from the right hemisphere components of the passive index to the left hemisphere components of BERT parse depth vector, suggesting that a sentence's structure represented in the left hemisphere might be influenced by the coarse estimate of the event plausibility concurrently determined by broad world knowledge in the right hemisphere (Jung-Beeman, 2005; see Figure 8—figure supplement 2 for more details).
evidence: This claim is supported by Granger causality analysis results shown in Figure 8E.

claim: In the Verb1 epoch, Verb1 transitivity obtained from either corpus data or human continuations did not exhibit significant model fits, which contrasted with the pronounced effects of BERT Verb1 parse depth.
source: In the Verb1 epoch, we tested Verb1 transitivity obtained from either corpus data or human continuations; however, neither of them exhibited significant model fits, which contrasted with the pronounced effects of BERT Verb1 parse depth (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the PP1 and MV epochs, the probabilities of PP and MV continuations, as determined from behavioural data, did not show any significant model fits.
source: Similarly, in the PP1 and MV epochs, the probabilities of PP and MV continuations, as determined from behavioural data, did not show any significant model fits (Figure 6—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: The effects of BERT parse depth vector in PP1 and MV epochs remained largely unchanged after controlling for the variance explained by the behavioural measures.
source: Furthermore, the effects of BERT parse depth vector in these two epochs (Figure 6B and C) remained largely unchanged after controlling for the variance explained by the behavioural measures.
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analyses shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: BERT structural measures, compared to corpus-based and behavioural measures, are better at fitting the neural dynamics during incremental speech comprehension.
source: These findings suggest that BERT structural measures, compared to corpus-based and behavioural measures, are better at fitting the neural dynamics during incremental speech comprehension. This might be attributed to the capacity of DLMs to capture more nuanced and contextually rich representations (Linzen and Baroni, 2021; Pavlick, 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of model fits, supported by citations to Linzen and Baroni, 2021 and Pavlick, 2022.

claim: The study revealed a shift from bi-hemispheric lateral frontal-temporal regions to left-lateralized regions in representing the current structured interpretation as a sentence unfolds.
source: Specifically, our results show (1) a shift from bi-hemispheric lateral frontal-temporal regions to left-lateralized regions in representing the current structured interpretation as a sentence unfolds
evidence: This is a summary of the spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results.

claim: The study revealed a pattern of sequential activations in the left lateral temporal regions, updating the structured interpretation as syntactic ambiguity is resolved.
source: (2) a pattern of sequential activations in the left lateral temporal regions, updating the structured interpretation as syntactic ambiguity is resolved
evidence: This is a summary of the spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results.

claim: The study revealed the influence of lexical interpretative coherence activated in the right hemisphere over the resolved sentence structure represented in the left hemisphere.
source: (3) the influence of lexical interpretative coherence activated in the right hemisphere over the resolved sentence structure represented in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a summary of the Granger causality analysis results.

claim: These findings provide empirical evidence for the constraint-based approach to sentence processing.
source: These findings provide empirical evidence for the constraint-based approach to sentence processing and deepen the understanding of specific spatiotemporal patterning and neuro-computational properties underpinning incremental speech comprehension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall pattern of results.

claim: Artificial neural networks have informed our understanding of various cognitive processes in the brain by providing quantifiable predictions that aim to connect behaviours and relevant neural activity.
source: ANNs have informed our understanding of various cognitive processes in the brain by providing quantifiable predictions that aim to connect behaviours and relevant neural activity (Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Rabovsky et al., 2018; Donhauser and Baillet, 2020; Yang et al., 2019; Kietzmann et al., 2019; Bao et al., 2020; Sheahan et al., 2021; Giordano et al., 2023; Doerig et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on ANNs and cognition.

claim: Recent studies have systematically compared the internal representations of deep language models to those observed in the human brain during language processing, which highlights the importance of predictive coding and contextual information.
source: Where DLMs are concerned, recent studies have systematically compared the internal representations of DLMs to those observed in the human brain during language processing, which highlights the importance of predictive coding and contextual information (Schrimpf et al., 2021; Goldstein et al., 2022; Heilbron et al., 2022; Toneva et al., 2022; Caucheteux et al., 2022; Caucheteux and King, 2022; Caucheteux et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple recent studies on brain-model alignment.

claim: BERT structural measures incorporate relevant lexical constraints and exhibit both behavioural and neural alignments with human listeners.
source: In line with this, our analyses confirmed that BERT structural measures incorporate relevant lexical constraints and that they exhibit both behavioural and neural alignments with human listeners.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation analyses presented in the Results section.

claim: Neural representations of an unfolding sentence's structure initially emerged in bilateral fronto-temporal regions and became left-lateralized when more complex syntactic properties were considered.
source: Specifically, neural representations of an unfolding sentence's structure initially emerged in bilateral fronto-temporal regions and became left-lateralized when more complex syntactic properties, rather than canonical linear adjacency, were considered to build a structured interpretation (e.g. beyond Verb1 in our stimulus sentences).
evidence: This is a summary of the spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results.

claim: In addition to the core fronto-temporal language network, the multiple-demand network and the default mode network were also involved during online construction of structured interpretations.
source: In addition to the core fronto-temporal language network, we found that the multiple-demand network and the DMN were also involved during online construction of structured interpretations, which may reflect additional cognitive demands for resolving potential structural ambiguity and evaluating the plausibility of underlying events (Smallwood et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatiotemporal searchlight RSA results and citation to Smallwood et al., 2021.

claim: Compared to corpus-based and behavioural measures, BERT structural measures are more effective in fitting listeners' neural activity, possibly due to its advanced ability in modelling specific contexts within each sentence.
source: Moreover, our results show that, compared to corpus-based and behavioural measures, BERT structural measures are more effective in fitting listeners' neural activity, possibly due to its advanced ability in modelling specific contexts within each sentence.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparison analyses and an inference about the reason for BERT's superior performance.

claim: Corpus-based and behavioural measures are crucial in interpreting BERT measures and understanding their alignment with listeners' neural activity.
source: Nevertheless, it is important to recognize the important role of corpus-based and behavioural measures as explanatory variables. They are crucial not only in interpreting BERT measures but also in understanding their alignment with listeners' neural activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach and the complementary roles of different types of measures.

claim: Unlike autoregressive deep language models, BERT is trained to predict masked words in a sentence with a bidirectional attention mechanism.
source: Firstly, unlike autoregressive DLMs trained using left-to-right attention and the next-word prediction task, BERT is trained to predict masked words in a sentence with a bidirectional attention mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement about the architecture and training of BERT, which is established knowledge.

claim: The bidirectional attention in BERT provides updated representations of preceding words every time an incoming word is added to the input.
source: The additional right-to-left attention provides updated representations of preceding words every time an incoming word is added to the input (e.g. representation of 'dog' in "The dog …" is different from that in "The dog found …").
evidence: This is a statement about how BERT's bidirectional attention works, which is established knowledge about the model.

claim: This feature of BERT is useful for tracking the dynamic change of the representation of a specific word as its context evolves.
source: This feature of BERT is useful for tracking the dynamic change of the representation of a specific word as its context evolves (e.g. Verb1 in this study), particularly in sentences with structural ambiguity.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of BERT's bidirectional attention for the current study.

claim: In autoregressive deep language models, the updated contextual effects are reflected in the hidden states of the right-most incoming word, while those of the preceding words on the left remain unchanged.
source: Although autoregressive DLMs also update hidden states as the input unfolds and could be used to study complex sentential structures (Jurayj et al., 2022), the updated contextual effects are reflected in the hidden states of the right-most incoming word, while those of the preceding words on the left remain unchanged (i.e. the representation of 'dog' is the same in "The dog …" and "The dog found …").
evidence: This is a statement about how autoregressive models work, which is established knowledge, with a citation to Jurayj et al., 2022.

claim: BERT processes two consecutive inputs independently, and there is no direct relationship between the hidden states of these two inputs.
source: Secondly, although we input each sentence word-by-word to BERT, however, unlike human listeners or recurrent neural networks, BERT process two consecutive inputs (e.g. "The dog …" and "The dog found …") independently, and there is no direct relationship between the hidden states of these two inputs.
evidence: This is a statement about how BERT processes sequential inputs, which is established knowledge about the model.

claim: Human listeners would not start over from the beginning of a sentence as it unfolds word-by-word, but update it continually as each word is heard.
source: In fact, human listeners would not start over from the beginning of a sentence as it unfolds word-by-word, but update it continually as each word is heard and use whatever information currently available to build a coherent interpretation (McRae and Matsuki, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McRae and Matsuki, 2013 and represents established knowledge about human sentence processing.

claim: For hypotheses such as parallel parsing, deep language models with recurrent memory might be more suitable than BERT.
source: Nonetheless, for other hypotheses in speech comprehension, such as parallel parsing and how various grammatically correct sentence structures are maintained and compete in the brain, DLMs with recurrent memory might be more suitable.
evidence: This is a speculation about which types of models might be better suited for different research questions.

claim: Future deep language models with more human-like model architecture and subjected to rigorous evaluation hold the potential to shed light on the neural implementation of various incremental processes that support the rapid transition from sound to meaning in the brain.
source: Future DLMs, especially those with more human-like model architecture (McClelland et al., 2020) and subjected to rigorous evaluation (Binz and Schulz, 2023), hold the potential to shed light on the neural implementation of various incremental processes that support the rapid transition from sound to meaning in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions, supported by citations to McClelland et al., 2020 and Binz and Schulz, 2023.

claim: Seventeen right-handed native British English speakers participated in this study.
source: Seventeen right-handed native British English speakers participated in this study and provided written consent.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the participants.

claim: One participant was excluded from subsequent analysis due to sleepiness during EMEG scanning.
source: One participant was excluded from subsequent analysis due to sleepiness during EMEG scanning, the other 16 participants were included in the following analyses (aged between 19 and 38 y, 26.5 y on average; seven females).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about participant exclusion.

claim: The sample size was determined according to previous MEG studies on speech comprehension.
source: This sample size was determined according to previous MEG studies on speech comprehension (Choi et al., 2021; Lyu et al., 2019; Klimovich-Gray et al., 2019; Kocagoncu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This study was approved by the Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee (reference number PRE2019.051).
source: This study was approved by the Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee (reference number PRE2019.051).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Verb1 in LoTrans sentences was selected to be optionally transitive according to CELEX and Google n-gram corpus.
source: Specifically, in the LoTrans sentences, Verb1 was selected to be optionally transitive according to CELEX (Baayen, 1993) and Google n-gram corpus (books.google.com/ngrams), meaning that it can either take a direct object or not.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about stimulus construction, supported by citations.

claim: Verb1 in HiTrans sentences had a higher preference for taking a direct object than Verb1 in LoTrans sentences (SCF probability for direct object: HiTrans 0.71 ± 0.16, LoTrans 0.44 ± 0.19, t(117) = 8.45, p=9.3 × 10–14).
source: Whereas Verb1 in HiTrans sentences was selected to have a higher preference for taking a direct object than Verb1 in LoTrans sentences [subcategorization frame (SCF) probability for direct object according to VALEX (Korhonen et al., 2006): HiTrans 0.71 ± 0.16, LoTrans 0.44 ± 0.19, two-tailed two-sample t-test, t(117) = 8.45, p=9.3 × 10–14].
evidence: This is a methodological statement about stimulus construction with statistical evidence, supported by citation to Korhonen et al., 2006.

claim: Structural probing models derived from BERT layer 14 showed the best overall performance.
source: Structural probing models derived from BERT layer 14 showed the best overall performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the performance evaluation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Additional structural probing models derived from BERT layers 12–13 and 15–16 were included in analyses to cover potentially useful downstream and upstream information.
source: However, additional structural probing models derived from its neighbouring layers (i.e. layers 12–13, 15–16 in the grey shade) were also included in further analyses to cover potentially useful downstream and upstream information.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about which BERT layers were used.
